title: When Do Better Schools Raise Housing Prices? Evidence from Paris Public and Private Schools
research_question: How does the academic performance of neighborhood public schools affect residential housing prices, and how does the local availability of private schools alter the magnitude of this relationship? Specifically, do private schools, by offering an alternative to residence-based public school assignment, attenuate the price premium that households pay to live in catchment areas of higher-performing public schools?
data_description: The study combines several administrative datasets covering the city of Paris over school years 1997–2004. Real estate data come from the BIEN dataset managed by the Paris Notary Chamber, containing approximately 200,000 arm's-length transactions of secondhand flats with detailed characteristics (size, age, number of rooms, floor, parking, etc.) and precise Lambert II geographic coordinates. School data come from the French Ministry of Education (SCOLARITE pupil records, OCEAN national exam database, IPES school characteristics) covering 108 public and 63 publicly funded private middle schools. Three school performance measures are constructed: average 2004 Diplôme National du Brevet exam scores, the share of pupils entering general curriculum high schools (1997–2004 average), and the share of pupils from privileged socio-economic backgrounds. Neighborhood socio-demographic controls come from the 1999 French National Census at the census block (Iris) level. The Paris LEA provided yearly maps of public middle school catchment area boundaries.
institutional_context: Secondary schooling in Paris during 1997–2004 combined strict residence-based assignment to public middle schools (collèges) with an extensive network of publicly subsidized private middle schools. Each public school catchment area contained exactly one school, and parents had little official latitude to choose another public school, though limited dispensations existed. The Paris Local Education Authority (Académie) centrally allocated teachers and resources, producing relatively homogeneous inputs across public schools, so observed performance differences largely reflected peer composition. Private schools, predominantly Catholic but driven mostly by educational rather than religious motives, are not subject to zoning, charge modest fees (roughly €500–€2000/year) due to State subsidies, freely select pupils citywide, and enrolled about one-third of Parisian middle schoolers. The State tightly restricts the opening of new private schools, making their geographic distribution highly stable over decades. Catchment boundaries often follow irregular zigzag patterns through otherwise similar neighborhoods, and most boundaries do not coincide with arrondissement administrative limits.
